name: Burj Khalifa
label: Burj Khalifa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Souk Al Bahar Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Souk Al Bahar Bridge' (node/7220965786): point; moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/446646206: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Burj Khalifa' (217 m across).
notes: The world's tallest building, seen best from Burj Park or the Dubai Fountain boardwalk.

text.description:
The Burj Khalifa is the world's tallest structure, at 829.8 m, and it opened in January 2010 as the centrepiece of Downtown Dubai. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed it with a Y-shaped floor plan, and its three wings step upwards to a slim spire. That tapering shape is what makes it so rewarding to photograph. From a good spot, the tower reads as one clean vertical line against the sky.

The best-known frame is from the Souk Al Bahar Bridge, a small footbridge over Burj Khalifa Lake. From here the tower rises behind the Dubai Fountain, with the water in the foreground and the Souk Al Bahar archways if you want a frame within the frame. It is free to stand there and works by day or during the evening fountain shows. It does get very crowded at show times, so arrive early and check the fountain schedule before you go.

If the bridge is too busy, Burj Park gives a wide, uncluttered view of the whole tower from base to tip. The Dubai Mall Waterfront Promenade shows the tower above the fountain, with Souk Al Bahar and the Downtown skyline around it.

The tower is so tall that you will need to step back or tilt your phone upwards to fit it in. Take a few frames at different distances, and keep the phone level so the sides do not lean inwards too much.
text.geographic_location: The Burj Khalifa stands in Downtown Dubai, beside the Dubai Mall and Burj Khalifa Lake, close to Sheikh Zayed Road. The Souk Al Bahar Bridge crosses the lake on the Souk Al Bahar side.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or other public transport stops are listed for this spot. The bridge is reachable on foot from the Dubai Mall and Souk Al Bahar area in Downtown Dubai, so head there first. From there, walk to the lake and find the small footbridge on the Souk Al Bahar side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower, the fountain and the lake in one frame. Then try the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the upper part of the tower or a tighter fountain-and-tower shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Souk Al Bahar Bridge (small footbridge over Burj Khalifa Lake, near the Souk Al Bahar side). The tower rising behind the Dubai Fountain, with the lake in the foreground and the Souk Al Bahar archways optionally in frame. The small footbridge over Burj Khalifa Lake near the Souk Al Bahar side. The tower rises behind the Dubai Fountain, with the lake in the foreground. If you like, include the Souk Al Bahar archways at the edge of the frame. For a wider, cleaner view of the whole tower, Burj Park is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line so it stands straight. Keep the lake in the lower third of the frame so the water and the fountain lead the eye upwards. If the bridge is crowded, hold the phone slightly higher than the heads in front of you. For a very different view, Burj Park or the Dubai Mall Waterfront Promenade are alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and the bright fountain lights do not wash out. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against the railing. Live Photos can capture the movement of the fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Arrive early for the evening fountain shows, as the bridge is very crowded at show times. Check the fountain schedule first. In daylight, early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the tower.

text.access_note: The Souk Al Bahar Bridge is a free public footbridge, but going up the tower itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Palm Jumeirah
label: Palm Jumeirah
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The View at The Palm' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'One at Palm by Omniyat' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/874795235: large area 'Palm Jumeirah' (7465 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Palm-shaped artificial island, best seen from above.

text.description: Palm Jumeirah is an island built from the sea in the shape of a palm tree: a trunk, a set of fronds and an outer crescent that curves around the top. Building began in June 2001, and the Dutch dredging company Van Oord carried out the work. Today the trunk is mixed shops and homes, the fronds are villas, and the crescent holds the big resorts, with around 30 hotels on the trunk and crescent as of 2024. The shape is the whole point, and it is easiest to read from height. The best way to photograph it is from above. The View at The Palm is the open-air terrace and glass barrier on the upper levels of the Palm Tower. From about 240 m up you can see the crescent, the fronds and the trunk laid out below, with Dubai Marina and the downtown skyline in the distance. Guides often treat it as the standard Palm photo spot, and the shot at the glass barrier is the one most people come for. Two ground-level alternatives are Palm Jumeirah Corniche, for the Marina and Jumeirah Beach Residence skyline across the water, and The Pointe, for Atlantis The Palm against the sea and sky. Drone flying over the Palm is heavily restricted, so don't plan an aerial shot from the ground. The terrace is the realistic way to get one.
text.geographic_location: Palm Jumeirah is the palm-shaped island off the Jumeirah coast, on the Gulf side of Dubai. Dubai Marina is visible across the water from the viewpoint. The viewpoint is in the Palm Tower on the island itself.
text.directions_text: There is no railway or tram stop to start from, so go by taxi or car and ask for The View at The Palm in the Palm Tower. The island's monorail runs from Gateway Towers at the foot of the island to Atlantis, but check the route before relying on it. Once inside the tower, head up to the observation levels. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole palm shape, crescent included, into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view of the skyline. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Dubai Marina or the towers in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at The View at The Palm (open-air terrace and glass barrier on the upper observation levels of the Palm Tower). The whole palm-shaped island from about 240 m up, with the crescent, fronds and trunk laid out below and the Dubai Marina and downtown skyline in the distance. At the glass barrier on the open-air terrace of the upper observation levels of the Palm Tower. From here the island's trunk, fronds and crescent lie below you. Dubai Marina and the downtown skyline sit in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the trunk with a vertical line so the fronds spread evenly either side. Keep the whole crescent in the frame, because that is what makes the shot recognisable. If you want something different, Palm Jumeirah Corniche gives a view of the Marina skyline across the water, with the Palm's shoreline in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the island to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone close to the glass, without pressing hard, to cut reflections. Try a Live Photo or a panorama if you want to take in the whole sweep of the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is the time guides recommend, but sunset slots cost more and sell out, so book ahead. After the light fades, use night mode and brace your elbows on the barrier to keep the phone steady.

text.access_note: The View at The Palm is a ticketed attraction and sunset slots sell out, so check the official site before you go and book in advance.

name: Burj Al Arab
label: Burj Al Arab
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Souk Madinat Jumeirah' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Car Parking - Souk Madinat Jumeirah' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/12700546: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jumeirah Burj Al Arab' (131 m across).
notes: Sail-shaped luxury hotel on its own island, seen from Jumeirah Public Beach.

text.description: Burj Al Arab is the sail-shaped hotel that stands on its own artificial island off the Jumeirah coast. It opened on 1 December 1999 and is about 321 m tall. The shape is meant to recall the sail of a dhow, and the translucent fibreglass facade is lit up at night, so the hotel looks different at dusk than at midday. The island sits roughly 280 m offshore and is linked to the land by a private curving bridge, so you photograph it from a distance rather than from its doorstep. From the outdoor areas along the canals and the open-air dining terraces, the hotel appears in the distance, framed by the souk's arches, waterways and traditional Arabian architecture. The old-style foreground against the modern sail makes the picture. If you want a clean side profile instead, Umm Suqeim Beach and Umm Suqeim Park are the alternatives. The hotel is currently closed for renovation, due to run until 31 October 2027, so check what the exterior looks like before planning a special trip. Take a few frames at different zoom levels and pick the one where the arches and the tower balance best.
text.geographic_location: Burj Al Arab sits on its own island just off Jumeirah Beach, on Dubai's Gulf coast.
text.directions_text: There is no Metro or tram stop at this spot, so the easiest way is by taxi or a navigation app to Souk Madinat Jumeirah, on the Jumeirah coast. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the arches, the water and the hotel together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the sail. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are standing close to an arch and want it to frame the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Souk Madinat Jumeirah (outdoor areas along the canals and open-air dining terraces). The hotel seen in the distance, framed by the souk's arches, waterways and traditional Arabian architecture. On the outdoor walkways by the canals or on the open-air dining terraces.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use an arch as a natural frame and place the hotel in the opening, with the canal as a leading line below it. Turn on gridlines and keep the tower on one of the vertical lines so it stays upright. If you want a plain side view of the sail above the sea, Umm Suqeim Beach is the alternative, and Umm Suqeim Park gives the hotel behind lawns and paths.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hotel to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the sail. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or rail to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually works well, when the sky softens and the hotel's lighting starts to show. Check on the day, as conditions vary.

text.access_note: The souk's outdoor areas are free to walk around, but the hotel itself is private and currently closed, and shoreline access nearby can be limited, so check the official site and local signs before you go.

name: The Dubai Mall
label: Dubai Mall
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18195959: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Dubai Mall' (1006 m across).
notes: One of the world's largest shopping malls, with an aquarium and the fountain promenade.

text.description:
Dubai Mall is the largest shopping mall in Dubai, part of Downtown Dubai and right next to the Burj Khalifa. It opened on 4 November 2008 and now has over 1,200 shops, so it works as a whole day out as much as a photo stop. It also drew a record 105 million visitors in 2023.

For a phone photographer the appeal is variety under one roof. There are tall, bright atriums, long shopfront corridors, a replica of the Dubai Creek Tower in the Grand Atrium, and a Diplodocus fossil known as the Dubai Dino, which is about 24 metres long and over 7 metres high. The Dubai Aquarium & Underwater Zoo shows more than 300 species of marine animals, including sharks and rays. Outside the building, near the Burj Khalifa, the Dubai Fountain runs water shows set to music and lights.

The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the mall, so treat it as a starting place for exploring the interior. Look for open spaces with a clear view up or along the length of a hall, and wait a moment for a gap in the crowds. Shoot a wide scene first, then move closer for details such as the dinosaur skeleton or shop lighting. Use the gridlines to keep verticals straight, because tall interiors look tilted very easily.
text.geographic_location: Dubai Mall is in Downtown Dubai, immediately beside the Burj Khalifa.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Downtown Dubai, next to the Burj Khalifa, and ask for Dubai Mall. Once inside, head for the middle of the building, where the phone icon on the map is. It is a large mall, so allow extra time to walk through it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for tall atriums and big open halls, and the default lens (1x) for shopfronts, people and general scenes. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the Dubai Dino, fish in the aquarium or decorative lighting.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with pillars, glass edges or shop fronts so the verticals stay straight. Hold the phone level and keep it at chest height for the ultra-wide, so the ceiling and floor both fit without distortion. For the Dubai Dino or the Dubai Creek Tower replica, step back and use 1x or 2x so the whole object is in view. If you want the Dubai Fountain outside as well, take that as a separate shot near the Burj Khalifa.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so shop lights and skylights do not burn out. Use portrait mode for friends or family against a busy background. Switch on night mode only if the lighting is dim, and hold still while it works.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Quieter hours give you cleaner views with fewer people in the frame. For the fountain outside, wait until after dark for the lights and music.

text.access_note: Dubai Mall is a public shopping centre, but some attractions inside, such as the aquarium, are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Quieter hours, such as early on a weekday, usually mean fewer people in photos.
The Dubai Fountain is best seen after dark when its lights are most visible.

name: Atlantis, The Palm
label: Atlantis The Palm
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/89790675: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Atlantis Hotel' (349 m across).
notes: Resort at the top of the Palm Jumeirah crescent.

text.description:
Atlantis, The Palm is the big resort at the apex of Palm Jumeirah, the first resort built on the island. It opened on 24 September 2008 and is themed on the myth of Atlantis, with some Arabian touches mixed in. The hotel has 1,544 rooms in two accommodation wings, the East Tower and the West Tower. The Aquaventure water park and the Lost Chambers Aquarium sit alongside it. The main building is 23 storeys high.

It photographs well because of its sheer scale. The two towers and the wide span between them make a strong, symmetrical shape that is easy to recognise in a picture.

For a phone, start with the default lens (1x) and keep the phone level so the towers do not lean. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want both wings in one frame. Add a foreground, such as palms, a path or the water's edge, to give the picture some depth. Check the building is fully in the frame before you press the shutter, because the edges are easy to clip.
text.geographic_location: At the apex of Palm Jumeirah, the man-made palm-shaped island off the Dubai coast. It is at the apex of the island.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed nearby; check a map app for the best way to reach the Atlantis end of Palm Jumeirah, the apex of the island. Then head for the phone icon on the map. From there the hotel is 259 m to the north-west, a short walk. Follow the map rather than guessing at roads. The phone icon on the map is about 180 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the hotel. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit both towers in. Telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for tighter shots of the roofline and the upper part of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 180 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Face north-west and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they stand straight. Include something in the foreground, such as palms, paving or water, to give a sense of scale. Take one wide shot with the whole building, then one closer with 2x or more for detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and the facade keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something steady, as it needs a second or two of stillness.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or the hour before sunset gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows. Dusk, when the building is lit, suits night mode.

text.access_note: The resort is a private hotel with ticketed attractions such as Aquaventure and the Lost Chambers Aquarium, so check the official site before you go for what the public can enter.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point looks north-west towards the hotel, so the morning sun is roughly behind the photographer and lights the front of the building.
Morning and the hour before sunset usually give softer light than midday in Dubai.
The building is lit after dark, which suits night mode.
Palms, paving or water may be available as a foreground at the stand-here point.

name: Dubai Gold Souk
label: Gold Souk
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Deira Old Souk Abra Station' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Deira Old Souk' (pois).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Dubai Gold Souk'.
notes: Arcaded market in Deira with dozens of gold shops.

text.description:
The Dubai Gold Souk is a traditional market in Deira, on the Al Ras side of Dubai Creek. It has more than 380 retailers, most of them jewellery traders selling gold, platinum and silver pieces, plus bullion and loose stones. Some shops are around forty years old, while others are newer. The market began informally in the early 1900s, when a handful of merchants set up beside the creek, and it grew through the mid-twentieth century as Dubai's trading climate drew merchants from India and Iran. It once held the world's largest ring, weighing 64 kg.

It is a general view rather than one exact spot, so take a few steps along the bank and check the framing as you go. The abras give you movement and colour in the foreground, and the water adds depth.

For the market itself, walk north to the arched entrance, the classic opening frame, with shopfronts and shoppers passing through. Inside, the alleys suit street and detail shots. Ask shopkeepers before photographing their displays, and don't plan on using a tripod in the covered market. Renovation of the souk was announced for the near future, so the look may change.
text.geographic_location: In Deira, on the Al Ras side of Dubai Creek, in Dubai's older commercial district. The souk sits close to the Deira Corniche and Baniyas Square, with the Dubai Fish and Vegetable Market to its north.
text.directions_text: Head to Deira and ask for the Deira Old Souk Abra Station on the Dubai Creek bank. From there the souk entrance lies to the north, about 500 m on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the creek and waterfront. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the souk's arched entrance if it is crowded, and to telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out abras or shop details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Deira Old Souk Abra Station (Dubai Creek bank, looking across the water towards the souk district). A creek-side view with abras and the old Deira waterfront, with the Spice and Gold Souk area sitting behind the waterfront as a backdrop. On the Dubai Creek bank, and look across the water towards the souk district. The souk's arched entrance lies to the north of here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the waterline on a lower third, with an abra as your foreground subject and the buildings behind. Keep the horizon level. As an alternative, walk north to the Dubai Gold Souk's arched entrance and frame the shopfronts and passing shoppers through the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on an abra to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky and water don't wash out. Inside the souk, tap on a window display and lower the exposure a little so the gold doesn't blow out. Hold the phone steady with both hands and ask before photographing a shopkeeper's display.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the creek and fewer people at the water's edge. Check the souk's current opening times before you go.

text.access_note: The creek bank is a public waterside space, but the souk is a working market whose access and rules may change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Museum of the Future
label: Museum of the Future
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sheikh Zayed Road' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'TAZA Sheikh Zayed Restaurant' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/33875310: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum of the Future' (273 m across).
notes: Torus-shaped building covered in Arabic calligraphy.

text.description:
The Museum of the Future is a silver, ring-shaped building in Dubai's Financial District, with Arabic calligraphy cut through its shell as windows. The lettering carries three quotes from Dubai's ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, about the future and innovation. The script was written by the Emirati artist Matar Bin Lahej. The shell is made of 1,024 steel-clad panels, each with its own 3D shape, and the museum opened on 22 February 2022. It has seven floors.

It photographs well because the shape is so simple and so unusual. The calligraphy gives you lines and texture, and the building stands out clearly against the towers of Sheikh Zayed Road. The classic exterior photo is taken from the far side of the highway, directly opposite, where the lettering is readable and the twin Emirates Towers frame the view. If you want a different angle, the pedestrian bridge at Emirates Towers Metro Station gives a higher, wider view that suits symmetrical and night shots.

Keep the whole ring in the frame and leave a little space around it, so the curve reads as a complete shape. Wait for a gap in the traffic and any passers-by if you want a cleaner picture. Photography is allowed inside the museum, but the viewpoints described here are outdoors and free.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the Financial District of Dubai, beside Sheikh Zayed Road. The best exterior view is from the far side of the highway, opposite the building and close to the Emirates Towers.
text.directions_text: Head for the Financial District along Sheikh Zayed Road. The classic viewpoint is reached via the Emirates Towers Metro Station pedestrian crossing, which takes you to the far side of the highway, directly opposite the museum. Never cross Sheikh Zayed Road on foot through the traffic. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the whole ring with the towers around it. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the calligraphy, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) from the pedestrian bridge if you want more of the skyline and road.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Sheikh Zayed Road (far side of the highway, directly opposite the museum, reached by the Emirates Towers Metro pedestrian crossing). The full torus-shaped building with its calligraphy facade, set against the Sheikh Zayed Road skyline and the twin Emirates Towers. The classic viewpoint is on the far side of Sheikh Zayed Road, directly opposite the museum, reached via the Emirates Towers Metro pedestrian crossing. From there you can see the full torus-shaped building with its calligraphy facade, set against the Sheikh Zayed Road skyline and the twin Emirates Towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and centre the ring on the middle lines, or place it slightly off-centre with a tower on one side. Keep your phone level so the verticals of the towers stay straight. As an alternative, the Emirates Towers Metro Station pedestrian bridge gives an elevated, wide view that works well for symmetrical and night compositions.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the glowing lettering to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lit calligraphy is not washed out. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows on a railing or wall to keep the phone steady. Take a few frames, as passing traffic can blur some of them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset to blue hour, when the calligraphy is backlit and the sky still has some colour.

text.access_note: The outside viewpoints are on public streets and walkways and are free, but entry to the museum itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Dubai Frame
label: Dubai Frame
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Zabeel Park' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Dinosaur Park Dubai Zabeel' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/386649647: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Dubai Frame' (103 m across).
notes: Giant picture-frame landmark in Zabeel Park with views of old and new Dubai.

text.description:
The Dubai Frame is a huge picture frame you can photograph from across the park. It stands 150.24 m tall and 95.53 m wide, and holds the record for the largest frame in the world. It opened in January 2018 and works as an observatory, museum and monument. The proportions follow the golden rectangle. The cladding is gold-coloured, so it stands out clearly against the sky and the greenery around it.

The best wide view is from Zabeel Park, on the main lawn near Gate 4, where you can stand well back and fit the whole structure in. Palms and flower beds make a natural foreground, and the lawn gives you room to walk backwards until nothing is cut off. Crouching low makes the Frame look taller. Late afternoon or golden hour is when the gold glows most.

If you want a different angle, try the reflecting pool at the foot of the Frame for a low shot with its mirror image, or the footbridge opposite the entrance for a head-on view from above the road. The pool is by the entrance, so it may be busy.

The Frame was built to show old Dubai on one side (Deira, Umm Hurair and Karama) and the modern towers of Sheikh Zayed Road on the other. That idea is worth keeping in mind when you choose what to include in the shot.
text.geographic_location: The Dubai Frame is in Zabeel Park, Dubai, near the Star Gate of the park. Sheikh Zayed Road's towers are on one side, and Deira, Umm Hurair and Karama on the other.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the best way to reach Zabeel Park. For the best wide view, the recommended viewpoint is the park's main lawn near Gate 4. Walk towards the Frame and stop when the whole structure still fits comfortably in your screen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole Frame with lawn and palms in front. If you are close and the top is cut off, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). If you want a tighter, cleaner shot of the Frame alone, try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Zabeel Park (main lawn near Gate 4, walked back from the base). The full 150 m golden frame set against the park lawn, with palms and flower beds in the foreground. The recommended viewpoint is the main lawn of Zabeel Park, near Gate 4, with the Frame to the north. From the lawn you see the full golden frame against the grass, with palms and flower beds in the foreground. Stay well back so the whole structure fits.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the two uprights with the vertical lines so the Frame does not lean. Crouch low and hold the phone near the ground to make the Frame look taller, and use the flower beds and palms as foreground. For a variation, the reflecting pool at the foot of the Frame gives a low shot with its reflection, and the footbridge opposite the entrance gives a head-on view from above.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Frame to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Keep your phone level, as tilting it distorts the shape of the Frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or golden hour, when the gold cladding glows.

text.access_note: The Frame sits inside Zabeel Park and going up it is a visitor attraction with limited numbers, so check the official site before you go for entry and ticket details.

name: Dubai Marina
label: Dubai Marina
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bluewaters Island' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bluewaters Island' (node/6358621691): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11912728: large area 'Dubai Marina' (4673 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Canal-side skyscraper district with a waterfront promenade.

text.description:
Dubai Marina is a district of tall towers built around an artificial canal that runs for about 3 km along the Gulf shoreline. The canal was dug out of the desert and filled with water from the Gulf. Most of the skyscrapers in the second phase stand between 250 and 300 metres tall, and Ciel Dubai Marina reaches 366 metres. Cayan Tower has a twisting shape. The Walk at Jumeirah Beach Residence (JBR), a 1.7 km strip of ground-level promenade, opened in 2008 and has been a tourist draw ever since.

The towers are packed so tightly that the whole cluster reads as one skyline, and that is what makes the classic shot work. From the western promenade you look across the water at the full row of towers, with the Gulf in the foreground. The Marina is about two kilometres away, so this is a skyline view rather than a close-up. The promenade is wide, so you can usually find a clear angle. If you want the towers reflected in the water, Marina Walk beside the canal is a good second choice. Take a few frames at different times if you can: the towers change a lot between late afternoon and after dark.
text.geographic_location: Dubai Marina is on the Gulf coast in the west of Dubai, between the Jebel Ali Port side and the Dubai Internet City and Media City area.
text.directions_text: From JBR Beach, cross the pedestrian bridge on foot to Bluewaters Island. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole row of towers with the sea in front. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of water or sky, as it makes the towers look small and far away. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a tighter group of buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bluewaters Island (western promenade of the island, facing the towers). The full Marina tower skyline lined up in front of the camera, with the Gulf in the foreground and the setting sun behind. On the western promenade, facing the towers. The Marina skyline sits in front of you with the Gulf below it, and the setting sun is behind you. Walk along the promenade until no railing, lamp post or passer-by cuts across the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the skyline on the upper third line, leaving the water as the lower two thirds. Keep the phone level so the towers don't lean. If you have time, take a second shot from Marina Walk, looking back across the canal at the towers and the yachts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. After sunset, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Aim to arrive about 45 minutes before sunset for the best light. Another good moment is 15-20 minutes after sunset, when the towers are lit up.

text.access_note: The promenade is an open public space reached on foot from JBR Beach, but check the official site before you go in case of closures or restrictions.

name: Ain Dubai
label: Ain Dubai
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Beach at JBR' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Eataly at The Beach Dubai' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1047288986: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ain Dubai' (248 m across).
notes: Giant observation wheel on Bluewaters Island.

text.description:
Ain Dubai is a giant observation wheel on Bluewaters Island, just off the Dubai coast. At 250 m it has been the world's tallest observation wheel since October 2021, and it is 82.4 m taller than the Las Vegas High Roller, the wheel it overtook. It was designed to carry up to 1,750 people in 48 cabins, with views towards Dubai Marina, Burj Al Arab, Palm Jumeirah and Burj Khalifa. Its name means 'eye of Dubai'.

The best way to photograph something this big is from a distance, where its full scale can sit against the buildings around it. The rock groynes at the western end of the public beachfront at JBR do exactly that. The wheel stands across the water with the Dubai Marina towers and the Gulf behind it. At sunset it often shows up as a silhouette against the sky. Bluewaters Island's pedestrian bridge is a good second spot, where the wheel is framed at the end of the walkway with the JBR towers behind.

The wheel closed to the public in 2022 and reopened to visitors on 26 December 2024, so its operating status has changed more than once. It stands there either way, and its LED displays have been lit at night, so it is worth a look after dark as well. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, and keep the sea in the foreground so the scale is clear.
text.geographic_location: Ain Dubai stands on Bluewaters Island, just off the coast opposite the JBR beachfront and close to Dubai Marina. The view across the water is from The Beach at JBR.
text.directions_text: Head for the public beachfront at JBR, next to Dubai Marina. Walk to the western end of the beach, where the rock groynes run out into the water. The wheel is to the north-west across the water. Bluewaters Island itself is reached by its pedestrian bridge, which makes a good second viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole wheel with the towers and sea around it. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot that makes the wheel look larger against the skyline. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the bridge, where you want the walkway leading to the wheel.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in The Beach at JBR (rock groynes at the western end of the public beachfront, facing across the water to the island). The wheel in full, standing about 700 m across the water with the Dubai Marina towers and the Gulf behind it, often as a silhouette against a sunset sky. From here the wheel is to the north-west across the water. You see all of it, with the Dubai Marina towers and the Gulf behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the wheel on one of the vertical lines so there is open sky and sea around it. Keep the horizon level. Include a little foreground, such as the rocks or the water's edge, to give a sense of scale. For a second view, walk to the Bluewaters Island pedestrian bridge and frame the wheel at the end of the walkway, with the JBR towers behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wheel to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little at sunset so the sky keeps its colour and the wheel stays a clean silhouette. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something solid, so the LED lights stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the wheel often stands out as a silhouette against the sky. The lights after dark are a good second choice.

text.access_note: The beachfront and groynes at JBR are public, but the wheel's operating status has changed, so check before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Beach at JBR is a public beachfront open to walkers.
The wheel often appears as a silhouette against a sunset sky from the western end of the beach.
The Bluewaters Island pedestrian bridge frames the wheel at the end of the walkway.
A telephoto lens compresses the view and makes the wheel look larger against the skyline.

name: Dubai Museum
label: Dubai Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2125281: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Housed in the 18th-century Al Fahidi Fort.

text.description: Dubai Museum is housed in Al Fahidi Fort, which was built in 1787 and is believed to be the oldest surviving building in Dubai. The museum opened in 1971 to show traditional life in the emirate. For photographs, the fort itself is the draw. It is square, with towers at three corners, and built of coral rock and mortar. Two cannons stand by the main gate on the eastern wall, with the flags of Dubai and the UAE above them. Inside, the central courtyard has a bronze cannon, a well, several boats and a traditional palm-frond summer house called an Arish, with its wind tower. Just outside the southern wall, a tall dhow stands in a large courtyard beside a reconstruction of the old city walls. Below ground, the galleries have life-size dioramas of a creek-side souk, desert life and a dhow being built. Start outside, where the pale walls, cannons and flags make a simple, clear picture. Then step into the courtyard for closer shots of the Arish, the boats and the well. Look for lines of towers and walls to give your pictures depth, and keep the dhow or the cannons in the foreground for scale. Indoors the light is low, so hold the phone steady with both hands. Check the official site before you go for current access and any photography rules.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Al Fahidi Fort, in the Al Fahidi area of Dubai.
text.directions_text: Head for the Al Fahidi area of Dubai and aim for Al Fahidi Fort, which is the museum building. Visitors can reach it by bus, metro, rented car or tour operator. Ask for Dubai Museum or Al Fahidi Fort. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is at the fort itself, so no further walk is needed. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the fort walls and the open courtyard. Use the default lens (1x) for the gate, cannons and flags. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the wind tower, the cannonballs and the textures of the coral rock.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, step back a little to fit the towers and walls in the frame, then move closer for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the fort walls and towers straight against them. Put a cannon or the dhow in the foreground to show scale, and let the flags sit in the upper part of the frame. In the courtyard, frame the Arish and its wind tower with boats or the well in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the walls, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the pale stone keeps its detail. Indoors, hold still, or try night mode if the phone offers it, and take a few frames to be sure one is sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the stone. Check the official site for opening times before you go.

text.access_note: This is a museum with a ticket office, so check the official site before you go for access, tickets and any photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer, with gentler shadows on pale stone walls.
Lighting in the underground galleries is likely to be low.
Photography rules inside the galleries may differ from those outdoors.

name: Dubai Creek
label: Dubai Creek
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Al Seef Park' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Skafos, Al Seef Dubai' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6525149: large area 'Dubai Creek' (13810 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic tidal inlet crossed by traditional abra boats.

text.description:
Dubai Creek is the natural saltwater inlet that gave the city its first harbour. It runs about 14 km inland from the Persian Gulf and is anywhere from 200 to 1,200 metres wide. For a long time it split the city into two halves, Bur Dubai and Deira, and wooden abras still carry people between them, which is what makes it so photogenic. From the creekside promenade at Al Seef Park you get old-style buildings and lanterns in the foreground, then the water, with boats crossing behind them.

Traders and fishermen worked from this waterway long before the towers arrived. Dredging began in the early 1960s, and Al Maktoum Bridge, the first crossing between the two banks, opened in 1963. That mix of working boats and heritage-style frontage gives you layers to play with: something close, something moving on the water, and the far bank beyond.

The creek is far too long to capture in one picture, so think of this as a scene rather than a landmark. Start with a close detail such as a lantern, a wooden rail or the prow of a boat. Then step back for a wider frame with the water and an abra crossing. If you can, come when the light is soft and low. Once the lanterns come on after dusk the same view looks quite different, so it is worth staying a little longer. The creek is a public waterway with boats working on it, so keep your phone and yourself well back from the water's edge.
text.geographic_location: Dubai Creek runs through the old heart of Dubai, between Bur Dubai and Deira.
text.directions_text: Head for the Al Seef waterfront and look for Al Seef Park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the abras, lanterns and old-style buildings together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole promenade and water, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a boat or the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Al Seef Park (creekside promenade along the Al Seef waterfront). Heritage-style waterfront with wooden abras crossing the creek behind a foreground of old-style buildings and lanterns. The picture shows the heritage-style waterfront with wooden abras crossing the creek behind a foreground of old-style buildings and lanterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put a lantern or a railing in the foreground, then let an abra cross the middle of the frame. Turn on gridlines and keep the water level with a horizontal line. For a different view, The Viewing Point shows the illuminated downtown skyline and Burj Khalifa across the water, and Al Shindagha gives open views along the creek toward the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the boat to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and lights do not wash out. Try a Live Photo while an abra passes and pick the best frame afterwards. After dusk use night mode and rest your elbows on a railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, then after dusk when the lanterns are lit.

text.access_note: Al Seef Park is an open public waterside promenade, but check the official site before you go in case anything has changed.

name: Madinat Jumeirah
label: Madinat Jumeirah
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Souk Madinat Jumeirah entrance bridge' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Car Parking - Souk Madinat Jumeirah' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1388000: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Resort with canals and wind towers, with a view of Burj Al Arab.

text.description:
Madinat Jumeirah is built to look like a traditional Arabian town, with gardens and canals. It is the largest resort in Dubai, covering over 40 hectares, and it holds three boutique hotels (Jumeirah Al Qasr, Jumeirah Mina A'Salam and Jumeirah Al Naseem) plus a courtyard of 29 summer houses. About 5.4 km of waterways link the different areas, and guests travel along them by abra, the traditional water taxi. That mix of water and old-style architecture is what makes it so easy to photograph.

The best free view is from the bridge directly outside the main entrance of the souk, in front of the gate. From there you can look along the canal, with its old-style walls and boats, and see the Burj Al Arab framed across the water behind it. It is not the full, unobstructed view of the hotel, but the canal in the foreground gives the picture depth and a strong sense of place, and you do not need to pay for an abra ride or go through the main doors to get it.

Keep the canal and its walls in the lower half of the frame and let the Burj Al Arab sit in the gap above. Other people on the bridge are likely to be in your shot, so be patient and take a few frames. If you want a different angle, Al Sufouh Beach gives a more distant view of the Burj Al Arab across the sand, with the Madinat Jumeirah wall behind the beach.
text.geographic_location: Madinat Jumeirah is on the Dubai coast, within sight of the Burj Al Arab. The souk entrance bridge is about 214 m east of the resort's mapped centre point.
text.directions_text: There are no listed Metro or tram stops for this spot, so a taxi is one option for reaching Madinat Jumeirah from central Dubai. Ask to be dropped at the Souk Madinat Jumeirah entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the canal with the Burj Al Arab behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the bridge and the souk gate in the frame. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the Burj Al Arab closer and squeeze the scene together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Souk Madinat Jumeirah entrance bridge (bridge directly outside the main entrance of the souk, in front of the gate; no official bridge name was found in the sources). The ancient-style canal in the foreground with the Burj Al Arab framed across the water behind it. Directly outside the main entrance of the souk and in front of the gate. From here the old-style canal runs in front of you and the Burj Al Arab is framed across the water behind it. The resort itself spreads out to the west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line. Keep the canal in the lower part of the frame as a leading line, and place the Burj Al Arab on a vertical third. Try one wide shot with the canal and walls, then one tighter zoomed shot of the hotel through the gap. For a different angle, Al Sufouh Beach shows the Burj Al Arab in the distance across the sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Burj Al Arab to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the building does not wash out. At dusk, use night mode and rest your elbows on the bridge rail to keep your hands steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light is softer, or around dusk. Mid-day sun is harsh and flattens the colours.

text.access_note: The bridge outside the souk entrance is a free place to stand and photograph, but access to the waterways inside the resort may need a booking or a guest visit, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon light is softer and mid-day sun is harsh for photos here.
The bridge is likely to have other visitors in the frame at busy times.
The Burj Al Arab is easy to pick out against the sky from the bridge.

name: Dubai Fountain
label: Dubai Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Souk Al Bahar Bridge' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Souk Al Bahar Bridge' (node/7220965786): point; moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/15670582: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Dubai Fountain' (350 m across).
notes: Choreographed fountain show on Burj Khalifa Lake, best after dark.

text.description:
The Dubai Fountain sits on the 12-hectare Burj Khalifa Lake in the middle of Downtown Dubai. It was designed by WET Design, the company behind the Bellagio fountains in Las Vegas, and opened on 8 May 2009 alongside the Dubai Mall. The display is 275 m long. It throws water as high as 152 m (500 ft) in time to music, and thousands of lights and colour projectors light it up. It photographs well because the Burj Khalifa rises straight behind the jets, so one frame gives you movement, water and the Burj Khalifa.

From midspan you look along the lake towards the fountain, a little above the crowd on the promenade. The bridge is also a busy walking route, so step to the side when you stop to shoot. The fountain closed for renovation in April 2025 and reopened on 1 October 2025, with more work planned for 2026. Show times change through the year, so check the current schedule before you plan your visit. If the bridge is too busy, the Dubai Mall Waterfront Promenade gives a close, low view, and Burj Park gives a wider one.
text.geographic_location: The fountain is on Burj Khalifa Lake in Downtown Dubai. The Souk Al Bahar Bridge is a pedestrian bridge facing the lake.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Downtown Dubai and walk to the Souk Al Bahar Bridge. Walk onto the pedestrian bridge and stop at midspan, facing the lake. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole lake, the jets and the full height of the Burj Khalifa. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter, calmer frame. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the jets or the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Souk Al Bahar Bridge (midspan of the pedestrian bridge, facing the lake). The fountain's jets in the foreground with the Burj Khalifa rising directly behind them, framed from slightly above the crowd. At midspan, facing the lake. From here the jets are in the foreground and the Burj Khalifa rises directly behind them, seen from slightly above the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the Burj Khalifa on a vertical line, with the jets in the lower third. Hold the phone upright to show the tower's height, or sideways to take in the full width of the show. If the bridge is crowded, try Burj Park for a wider view, or the Dubai Mall Waterfront Promenade for a close ground-level view. Check on the day which side of the lake gives the best backdrop, so walk around before the show starts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights and bright jets don't burn out. For moving water, try Live Photos or take several shots in a row and pick the best. Use night mode only if your phone copes well with movement, and rest your elbows on the rail to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the evening, when the lights are on and the shows run at regular intervals. Arrive a little early to find a spot on the bridge. Check the current show schedule first, because times change by season and during Ramadan.

text.access_note: The bridge is a free public walkway, but show times and any closures can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Saeed Al Maktoum House
label: Saeed Al Maktoum House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sheikh Saeed Al Maktoum House' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5755009: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saeed Al Maktoum House' (118 m across).
notes: Former royal residence in Al Shindagha, now a museum.

text.description:
Sheikh Saeed Al Maktoum House stands on the waterfront of Dubai Creek in Al Shindagha. It was built around 1896 as the seat of the Al Maktoum family and was the home of Sheikh Saeed bin Maktoum Al Maktoum, a former ruler of Dubai, until his death in 1958. Today it is a museum of old Dubai, with objects and photographs spread over nine wings. These cover the Al Maktoum family, marine life, social life, coins and stamps, and historic documents and maps. The building covers 3,600 square metres, so there is plenty to look at.

It photographs well for two reasons. From outside, the coral-stone walls, carved upper windows and wind towers give you a strong, textured old-Dubai subject. From the upper terraces and the majlis (the traditional sitting room), you get a wide view across the Creek to the modern city behind it. The terraces frame the old waterway against the new skyline in a single shot.

For your phone, the terraces are the main prize, so go inside and head up. Use the gridlines to keep the horizon straight. Let the terrace edges or openings frame the Creek, and tap the water or skyline to set focus. Outside, step back to fit the whole façade in, then zoom in on the carved windows and wind towers. If the sun is low, the walls should look warm and well modelled. Check the official site before you go, as the upper floors are reached through the museum.
text.geographic_location: In the Al Shindagha area of Dubai, on the waterfront of Dubai Creek.
text.directions_text: Make your own way to Al Shindagha on the Dubai Creek waterfront. The house is a large building right on the Creek, so it is easy to recognise once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the middle of the building, so once you are at the house you are already in the right place. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the terraces and in the majlis to take in the Creek, the skyline and the terrace framing together. Use the default lens (1x) for the main view across the water. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved upper windows and wind towers, or to pick out buildings on the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Go up to the upper floor terraces and the majlis, facing the Creek. From there you get a wide view over Dubai Creek with the modern city behind it, framed by the house's terraces.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the horizon of the far bank up with a horizontal line. Use the terrace openings or edges as a frame around the water and skyline. As an alternative, shoot the outside of the house, where the coral-stone walls, carved upper windows and wind towers catch the low sun.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the buildings and water keep their colour. Wipe the lens before shooting, as it picks up fingerprints easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low and warms the coral-stone walls. Museum visiting times will decide when you can reach the terraces, so check the official site before you go.

text.access_note: The house is a museum and the upper terraces and majlis are reached through the building, so check the official site before you go for opening times and entry details.

name: Jumeirah Mosque
label: Jumeirah Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jumeirah Beach Road' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Pearl Jumeirah Public Beach' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2298717: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Dubai's best-known mosque, open to visitors on guided tours.

text.description:
Jumeirah Mosque is one of the most recognisable religious buildings in Dubai, and the street view of its front is the classic postcard angle. It is built of yellow-pink sandstone, and its two minarets and central dome are covered in deep carved relief. The style draws on historic Islamic architecture, and official accounts name Fatimid design as the inspiration. Building began in 1975 and the mosque opened in 1979. It was a gift from Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum to his son, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum. It can hold up to 1,200 worshippers, and it appeared on the 2003 series of the 500 dirham note.

The building photographs well because the symmetry is strong. Seen square-on from across the road, the dome sits between the twin minarets with plenty of open sky behind, so the shot is simple to line up on a phone. Walk or ride from there to the street opposite the front of the mosque before you start shooting. The exterior can be photographed from the street. Keep worshippers out of your pictures, and ask first if you want a close-up of anyone. If you want a second angle, there is a view from the grounds with a minaret rising over the domes, framed by palm trees. Check access to the grounds before you go.
text.geographic_location: Jumeirah Mosque is in the Jumeirah district of Dubai, on the Persian Gulf side of the city. Its street-facing front looks onto the main road along the district's seafront, which may be signed as Jumeirah Beach Road or Jumeirah Street, so check the street signs on arrival.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed close to this spot. A taxi is the simplest general option: ask to be dropped on the main road opposite the mosque's street-facing front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the road, which shows the dome and both minarets together. If you are tight against the building or the road is narrow, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the minarets do not lean. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved detail on the minarets and dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jumeirah Beach Road (across from the main street-facing façade). The mosque's white dome and twin minarets seen square-on against the blue sky. From there the mosque is square-on in front of you. From across the road opposite the façade, the sandstone dome and twin minarets sit symmetrically against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the dome with the middle line, with a minaret roughly on each side. Keep the phone upright and level so the vertical lines stay straight. Leave some sky above the minarets. For a different angle, go to the grounds (check access first) and frame a minaret above the ribbed domes with palm trees, or shoot through the entrance archway to the dome and minarets behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mosque to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the sandstone keeps its detail. Hold the phone with both hands, as a tripod may not be allowed. Take a few frames, as passing traffic can spoil one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or about an hour before sunset, when the light is softer and warmer.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but entry is by guided tour only, with a modest dress code. Tour times vary and there are no tours on Fridays, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A taxi is a sensible general way to reach the street opposite the mosque, as no Underground or tram stop is listed nearby.
Keeping the phone level and using the grid helps stop the minarets leaning, especially with the ultra-wide lens.
Lowering the exposure slightly keeps the sky blue and preserves detail in the sandstone.
Passing traffic may spoil some frames.
The grounds viewpoint (minaret over the domes, entrance archway) may only be reachable as part of a visit, so access should be checked.

name: Dubai Spice Souk
label: Spice Souk
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Deira Old Souk Abra Station' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Deira Old Souk' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/542042596: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Spice Souk' (237 m across).
notes: Covered market in Deira with spices, incense and dried goods.

text.description:
The Dubai Spice Souk is a traditional market in Deira, made up of several narrow lanes lined with open and covered shops. Sacks and trays of spices, herbs, frankincense, incense and dried goods are set out at eye level, which makes it easy to fill a phone frame with colour and texture. Alongside the spices, shops also sell tea, textiles, rugs and household items, and most buying is done by haggling.

The souk sits on Baniyas Street in the Al Ras area, next to the Gold Souk and close to the Old Souk abra station on Dubai Creek. The map's stand-here point is the viewing position, a short walk south-east of the souk centre, and the nearby abra station landing is another good place to shoot from. The landing faces the souk entrance, so you can frame the shopfronts and their colourful sacks from the waterside edge, with abra boats and the creek nearby, and without stepping into the narrow lanes.

For a closer look, walk up to Baniyas Street, where heaped sacks and open trays sit right at the shopfronts with the covered lanes behind them. If you want a wider, higher view of the market's bustle, Dubai Municipality Museum is another place people mention. Check whether it is open to visitors before you go, as that is not confirmed.

Photography is generally allowed in the souks, but shopkeepers often object to close-ups that are not followed by a purchase. Ask first before photographing people or their goods, and stop if you are asked to. Drones are not practical in this heritage area.
text.geographic_location: In Deira, in eastern Dubai, in the Al Ras area along Baniyas Street. It sits next to the Gold Souk, close to the Old Souk abra station.
text.directions_text: Head for Al Ras in Deira, on Baniyas Street, and make for the Old Souk abra station on Dubai Creek. From there it is about 1 minute on foot to the middle of the souk, to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the shopfronts and sacks. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the souk entrance together with the abra boats and the creek. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as piles of spice, so you do not have to lean into a stall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Deira Old Souk Abra Station (landing directly facing the Spice Souk entrance). The spice shops and their colourful sacks framed from the waterside edge of the souk, with abra boats and the creek nearby. Nearby, the landing at Deira Old Souk Abra Station faces the Spice Souk entrance. From its waterside edge you can frame the spice shops and their colourful sacks, with abra boats and the creek beside them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the row of shopfronts on the lower third, with the creek or a boat in the foreground for depth. For a tighter shot, use the default lens (1x) and fill the frame with one stall's sacks. Baniyas Street is a good alternative for close, eye-level shots of heaped spices. Ask before photographing shopkeepers or their goods up close.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sacks to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright sky or sunlit stalls do not wash out the colours. A Live Photo can capture the movement of boats on the creek.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides recommend mornings, especially on weekdays, for softer light and fewer crowds. Light conditions vary, so be ready to adjust exposure.

text.access_note: The souk is an open, working market; photography is generally allowed, but ask vendors before close-ups and check the official site or local information before you go for shop times.

label: Al Fahidi / Bastakiya

notes: Old merchant quarter with wind-tower houses and narrow lanes.

text.description:
Al Fahidi Historical Neighbourhood, also known as Al Bastakiya, is the old quarter of Dubai, with low sand-coloured walls and narrow winding lanes. It dates back to the 1890s and was built largely by well-off Persian merchants. The name comes from the southern Iranian town of Bastak. In the 1980s about half of it was cleared for offices, and a demolition order in 1989 was cancelled after a British architect, Rayner Otter, campaigned to save it and showed Prince Charles around. A restoration project began in 2005.

For photos, one easy subject nearby is Al Fahidi Fort, the oldest surviving building in Dubai. You can shoot its exterior, but the museum inside has been closed for restoration, so plan on outside views only. Once you are in the lanes, the textures do the work: wall surfaces, decorative panels and Islamic-style windows. Dar Al Khatt Alarabi is a good place for a close, frontal shot of those details. Sheikh Saeed Al Maktoum House, on the Creek edge, shows the waterfront with the modern skyline beyond it. Take your time, as the lanes are narrow and other visitors will pass through your frame.
text.geographic_location: Al Fahidi Historical Neighbourhood is a historic district of Dubai. Sheikh Saeed Al Maktoum House is on the Creek edge.
text.directions_text: There are no Metro or tram stops listed for this spot, so check a map app for how to get there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the fort exterior and wider views. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in the tight lanes. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for window and wall details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Al Fahidi Fort (exterior, from the surrounding square). The oldest surviving building in Dubai, framed against the restored neighbourhood's low sand-coloured walls. Al Fahidi Fort, the oldest surviving building in Dubai, is a suggested subject for an exterior shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place your main subject, such as the fort exterior, on one third of the frame, leaving open space to fill the rest. Then walk into the lanes and fill the frame with window and wall textures, as at Dar Al Khatt Alarabi. For a second view, go to Sheikh Saeed Al Maktoum House and include the Creek and the skyline beyond it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a sunlit wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sand-coloured walls stay detailed and don't wash out to white.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and cooler walking. Visit early to avoid the busiest lanes.

text.access_note: The neighbourhood is a walkable historic district, but the fort and museum have been closed for restoration, so check the official site before you go.

name: Etihad Museum
label: Etihad Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Etihad Museum' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Etihad Museum'.
notes: Museum with a curved roof, marking the founding of the UAE.

text.description:
The Etihad Museum tells the story of how the United Arab Emirates came together as a country. It stands on the site where the rulers signed the union declaration, and where the first national flag was raised, on 2 December 1971. The old Union House, where that signing took place, is now part of the museum complex.

The building itself is the reason to bring your phone. Moriyama & Teshima Architects designed it in the shape of a manuscript, with seven columns that stand for the pens used to sign the declaration. The sweeping white roof is often described as echoing the parchment the constitution was written on. Seen whole from the lawn in front, it makes a clean, minimalist architectural photo: white curves, plenty of sky and very little clutter.

Take your time walking around the outside, because the roofline changes shape as you move. Start with one wide shot from the lawn, then step closer for details such as the columns and the edge of the roof. If you want a second view, the white plaza around Union House and the flagpole is a good alternative, with the reflecting pool and the round Union House behind it. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the long horizontal lines stay straight.

Photography rules inside the galleries seem to vary, so do not count on taking pictures indoors. The outdoor views are the reliable choice.
text.geographic_location: The Etihad Museum is in Dubai. The Union House on its site was formerly known as the Jumeirah Guesthouse.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check current transport options before you go. A taxi or car to the Etihad Museum is the simplest choice. Once there, walk to the outdoor lawn in front of the building. That is the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is about 1.6 km north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole curved white building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the roofline in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x) for details such as the columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 1.6 km north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Stand on the outdoor lawn in front of the Etihad Museum. From here you can see the curved white exterior and the roofline as a whole.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the roof up with the horizontal lines. Leave plenty of sky for a minimalist look. For a second picture, try the white plaza near Union House, with the flagpole above the reflecting pool and the round Union House behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white does not turn grey or lose its detail. If the roof will not fit in one shot, try panorama mode and move the phone slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light in the morning or late afternoon usually flatters white buildings. Strong midday sun can wash out the detail.

text.access_note: The exterior and lawn are outdoors, but the museum grounds, the Union House plaza and the galleries may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go, including its photography rules.
